paras: The whipping of Will Sewell was an attack on a Black farm hand in Pike County, Alabama, one night in April 1903, in which he was tied and beaten with a wagon whip by attackers the reports do not name. He was hurt badly enough that he could not work for three weeks. The whipping became public only in October 1903, as government testimony against six white men charged with whitecapping in the Cross Roads and Linwood beats, where Black residents had been ordered to leave, churches burned and a woman and her baby shot.

In September 1903 the Montgomery Advertiser's Troy correspondent reported "considerable excitement" over whitecappers in Cross Roads Beat, where hostility toward Black residents had led to "two or three personal conflicts." Written notices, many signed "Negro Skinner," ordered Black tenants and the Black hands of a steam sawmill to leave under threat of death, and most of them went. The sheriff went to the area to look for the authors, and the county grand jury, two of whose members had lost workers, was expected to investigate.

Federal authorities took up the matter, and in late October Deputy Marshal J. F. Green arrested six white farmers living about twelve miles from Troy: Boss Riley, William Pittman, Tumps Chesser and Robert, John and Fletcher Windham. They were accused of serving notices on Black residents, whipping "five or six negroes severely," and belonging to an organized gang that burned two churches and shot a woman and her baby.

Sewell's case was described at the preliminary hearing before U.S. Commissioner Tutwiler at Troy on October 30 and 31, held in the circuit court room because of the crowd. According to the Advertiser's account of the government evidence, Sewell was whipped one night in April "so severely that the blood ran from his wounds." He had been tied and beaten with a wagon whip, and "it was in evidence that he was whipped as a medicine and tonic," a phrase the report did not attribute to anyone. The report did not say where the whipping took place or which defendant, if any, was accused of it.

The same testimony covered the burning of Dunn's Chapel and Antioch church, a death notice left for Garfield Williams, the shooting into Joe Browning's house, and the shooting of Mary Clements and her baby as she fled her home.

Tutwiler discharged Robert Windham and held the other five for the federal grand jury, Fletcher Windham on $750 bail and the rest on $500 each. The Advertiser added that witnesses had been threatened and that the government had re-subpoenaed its witnesses so they could have its protection.

On January 27, 1904, the federal grand jury at Montgomery returned true bills against Riley, Pittman and the three Windhams for oppressing ten named Black residents "because they are of African descent." Sewell was not among the ten, and the charges centered on the threats, the church burnings and the attacks on Browning and Clements. The cases were set for the May term, but no report of a trial was found.

Only the Montgomery Advertiser named Sewell, in a long Troy special headed "Held to Grand Jury" that spoke of a "bad condition of affairs" in that part of Pike County. Its correspondent called the Black victims "quiet inoffensive negroes" and wrote that "the best element" of the county opposed such crimes because they tended "to cripple the farming." Outside Alabama, the Indianapolis Journal ran a short wire item on the arrests and the Atlanta Constitution a one-sentence notice of the binding over, neither of them mentioning the whipping. In January the New-York Tribune printed the indictments under the headline "Blacks Caught It Hard."

The St. Paul Appeal, a Black weekly, carried a Birmingham dispatch on the hearing under "Afro-Americans White-Capped. A Tale of Horror," within a monthly feature on white crime meant to show "no color line in crime." Its garbled account dwelt on the shooting of Mary Clements, a beating of Joe Browning and an estimate that 150 people had left the county, and it did not name Sewell.
